summary: Describes the data plane of the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP). LISP uses two namespaces, Endpoint Identifiers for hosts and Routing Locators for network attachment points, and routers exchange encapsulated packets based on them to build overlay networks. It obsoletes RFC 6830. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: LISP lets a network keep two different addresses for each host: one that says which host it is and never changes, and one that says where in the network the host can be reached right now. Routers at the edge of a site look up the second address and wrap the packet in a new header, so the ordinary internet in the middle never needs to understand the host's own address space.

subtitle: How LISP routers wrap ordinary packets so a host's identity and its network location stay separate.

tldr.problem: An IP address says both who a host is and where it is attached to the network, so moving a host or attaching it in two places forces changes throughout the routing system.
tldr.mechanism: LISP splits the address into an Endpoint Identifier, which says who the host is, and a Routing Locator, which says where it can be reached. Tunnel routers at the edge of a site look the second up from the first and wrap the packet in a new IP and UDP header before sending it across the underlay.
tldr.outcome: The RFC replaced RFC 6830 with a revised data plane, and it states that the two are not compatible with each other.

facts.label: Gleaned entry lifetime
facts.value: A recommended period of 3 seconds, pending verification

today: RFC 9300 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 6830, and the RFC states that the LISP data plane protocol is not backwards compatible with that document: the encapsulation changed, and there is no version field to negotiate it, so an implementation follows the control plane in RFC 9301 to learn which data plane a peer supports.

sections.title: Why Separate Identity from Location
sections.content:
LISP is an encapsulation protocol built on one idea: the topological location of a network attachment point should be separate from the identity of the node attached to it. That produces two namespaces. Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) identify end hosts, such as nodes or virtual machines. Routing Locators (RLOCs) identify the network attachment points where those hosts can be reached, and they are routable addresses in the underlay network.

LISP then defines functions for mapping between the two namespaces, and for carrying traffic from devices that use non-routable EIDs across a network that routes and forwards using RLOCs. The encapsulation is a dynamic form of tunneling: nothing has to be set up in advance, because the mapping is looked up when it is needed.

Nothing has to change in the hosts or in the underlay routers. The addresses a host uses to track its connections and to send packets do not change when LISP is in use, and the routers along the path keep doing ordinary forwarding lookups. Separating the EID from the RLOC space is what gives LISP traffic engineering, multihoming and mobility.

LISP was first motivated by the Internet-wide route scaling problem, but as it was developed a large number of other uses appeared, and the design now focuses on those. What they share is a set of cooperating entities that want to talk over the public Internet or another large underlay while keeping their own addressing and topology separate from the underlay's.
sections.plainLanguage: An IP address normally answers two questions at once: which host is this, and where do I send the packet. LISP splits those questions. One address says which host it is and stays the same. The other says where to send it now, and the routers at the edge of the network work out the second one from the first.

sections.title: The Vocabulary of LISP
sections.content:
An EID is a 32-bit value for IPv4 or a 128-bit value for IPv6 that identifies a host. It is generally found only in the source and destination address fields of the innermost LISP header. A host obtains a destination EID through a DNS lookup or a SIP exchange, and the source EID through the same mechanisms it uses to set its own local address. An EID used on the public Internet must be unique, like any other address used there, and it is allocated to a host from a block of EIDs given to the site where the host lives.

An RLOC is an IPv4 or IPv6 address of an Egress Tunnel Router. It is the result of an EID-to-RLOC lookup, and an EID maps to zero or more RLOCs. RLOCs are numbered from blocks assigned to a site at each point where it attaches to the underlay network, so they follow the shape of the provider's topology.

The routers at the edge of a site are tunnel routers. The one that receives traffic leaving the site is the Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR); it treats the destination address as an EID, looks up an RLOC for it, and puts a new outer IP header on the packet with one of its own RLOCs as the source and the looked-up RLOC as the destination. The one that receives traffic arriving at the site is the Egress Tunnel Router (ETR); it strips the outer header and forwards the packet on the strength of the next IP header. The term xTR refers to either one when the direction of the flow does not matter. A LISP site is a set of routers in an edge network under a single technical administration.

An ITR keeps its mappings in an EID-to-RLOC Map-Cache, an on-demand table that is local, dynamic and relatively small, and whose entries expire according to their time to live. It is distinct from the EID-to-RLOC database, which is distributed, relatively static and holds every known mapping.

Where an address space has to be kept separate, such as with overlapping addresses or multi-tenant virtualization, an Instance ID is used. The ITR copies a 24-bit value into the Instance ID field of the LISP header, and the ETR uses it as a table identifier when it looks up the inner destination EID. The source and destination EIDs must belong to the same Instance ID.
sections.plainLanguage: The names LISP uses are worth knowing. An EID says which host you are talking to. An RLOC says which router to send the packet to in order to reach that host. The ITR is the router that wraps the packet, the ETR is the router that unwraps it, and the Map-Cache is where the ITR remembers which RLOCs belong to which EIDs.

sections.title: How a Packet Crosses the Network
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the case of a host at one site, host1.abc.example.com, opening a TCP connection to host2.xyz.example.com at another site, exactly as it would if the sites did not use LISP. Each site is multihomed, so each tunnel router has an RLOC from the service provider's address block for each provider it is attached to.

The host does a DNS lookup and receives an A or AAAA record. That address is the destination EID, and the host's own local address is the source EID. The packet is built and forwarded through the source site as an ordinary IP packet until it reaches the ITR.

The ITR must map the destination EID to an RLOC of one of the ETRs at the destination site. A Map-Request, as specified in the LISP control plane, asks for that mapping; the mapping system forwards it to the corresponding ETR. The ETR matches the destination EID against the prefixes in its mapping database for the site it serves. If there is no match, the request is dropped. Otherwise a Map-Reply is returned to the ITR, which stores the mapping in its Map-Cache.

Every later packet to the same destination gets a LISP header prepended by the ITR, with the RLOC learned from the ETR as the header's destination address. The packet may go to a different ETR than the one that answered, because of the source site's hashing policy or the destination site's Locator-Set policy. The ETR receives the packets directly, since the destination address is one of its own, checks the addresses, strips the LISP header and forwards the packets to the destination host.

To save a mapping lookup in the reverse direction, it is optional for an ETR to create a cache entry that maps the source EID in the inner header to the source RLOC in the outer header. Such an entry is called a glean mapping and holds a single RLOC.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet leaves the source site as an ordinary IP packet. When it reaches the edge router, that router asks the mapping system where the destination host can be reached, wraps the packet in a new header addressed to that place, and sends it across the internet. The router at the far end takes the new header off and delivers the original packet.

sections.title: The Encapsulated Packet
sections.content:
The LISP header is the outer IPv4 or IPv6 header, a UDP header, and a LISP-specific 8-octet header that follows the UDP header. The ITR prepends those headers and the ETR strips them. The outer header carries RLOCs, the inner header is the one the host sent and carries EIDs, and the outer header's IP protocol number is UDP (17).

The UDP destination port must be the well-known IANA-assigned value 4341. The source port is chosen by the ITR, and the UDP checksum should be sent as zero by the ITR for either IPv4 or IPv6 encapsulation. An ETR must accept a packet with a zero checksum for decapsulation. When an ITR sends a non-zero value it must compute it correctly, and an ETR that receives a non-zero value may verify it, in which case a failed verification means the packet is silently dropped.

The 8-octet LISP header holds eight flag bits and two more fields. The N-bit says a nonce is present in the low-order 24 bits of the first 32-bit field; the L-bit says the Locator-Status-Bits in the second 32-bit field are in use; the E-bit asks for the nonce to be echoed back; the V-bit says the first field holds a Map-Version instead of a nonce, and the N-bit must then be zero; the I-bit says the high-order 24 bits of the second field are an Instance ID, leaving 8 bits for Locator-Status-Bits; the R-bit is reserved and must be zero; and the KK-bits are a 2-bit key identifier used when encapsulated packets are encrypted, set to 00 when they are not. The N-bit and the V-bit must not both be set in the same packet, and if they are, a decapsulating ETR treats the field as holding a nonce.

The time to live of the outer header should be copied from the inner header, and an ETR must copy the inner time to live from the outer one when the outer value is smaller, which preserves the distance the host intended the packet to travel and suppresses looping packets when tunnels are concatenated by mistake. The DSCP value should be copied in both directions, while the ECN bits need special treatment to avoid losing congestion indications.

Since IPv4 and IPv6 addresses can each be EIDs or RLOCs, all four combinations are supported: IPv4 inside IPv4, IPv6 inside IPv6, and the two mixed forms.
sections.plainLanguage: The added headers are an ordinary IP header, a UDP header and eight bytes of LISP-specific flags. The UDP port number tells the far side that this is a LISP packet, and the flags say whether the packet carries a nonce, whether the locators are up or down, and which address space inside the site it belongs to.

sections.title: Choosing a Locator
sections.content:
The Map-Cache holds the state an ITR uses to encapsulate packets. A longest-prefix match of the EID against the cache returns a Locator-Set, a list of RLOCs for the EID's topological location. Each RLOC in the set carries a Priority and a Weight. The RLOC with the lowest Priority is chosen, and an RLOC with Priority 255 must not be used for forwarding. When several RLOCs share the same Priority, the Weight says how the traffic is shared among them.

Who controls the choice depends on the case. If the server side returns one RLOC, the client side has no choice. If it returns a list of which a subset has the best Priority, the client must use that subset and the server controls both the subset and the split of traffic across it, although the client may fall back to RLOCs outside the subset if it finds them unreachable. If the server sets a Weight of zero for the subset, the client decides how to spread the load.

Either side may instead glean the RLOCs from the packets it receives. In that case the server-side ETR takes on the job of deciding which client locators work, and it must assume that each client RLOC has the same best Priority with a Weight of zero. A gleaned Map-Cache entry is only stored and used for a recommended period of 3 seconds, pending verification, and verification is done by sending a Map-Request for the source EID of the received packet. Gleaning must not be used over the public Internet.

For load-sharing, the RFC describes a hash algorithm an ITR may use. It may hash the source and destination addresses, or use the common 5-tuple hash of the source and destination addresses, the source and destination TCP, UDP or SCTP port numbers, and the protocol number; for a packet that is not TCP, UDP or SCTP, only the addresses are used. The hash value is divided by the number of locators in the Locator-Set, and the remainder, from 0 to one less than the number of locators, selects the locator. The source port of the outer UDP header should be the same for all packets of one flow, so that core routers attached to link aggregation groups can spread the encapsulated packets across the member links instead of seeing a single flow.
sections.plainLanguage: When a host has more than one way of being reached, the mapping says which way is preferred and how the traffic should be shared. The sending router picks one address, either by following those instructions or by hashing the packet so that the load spreads out.

sections.title: Packets That Are Too Big
sections.content:
Because tunnel headers are added, a packet can end up larger than the largest packet any link between the ITR and the ETR can carry. The RFC proposes two mechanisms for dealing with this, and leaves the choice to the implementor: both may be used, neither may be used, and sites with different mechanisms can interoperate.

The stateless mechanism defines three quantities. H is the size in octets of the outer header the ITR prepends, including the UDP and LISP headers. L is the largest packet the ITR can send to an ETR without the ITR or any intermediate router having to fragment it. S is an architectural constant for the largest packet the ITR must accept from the source, so that L = S + H. When a packet from a site-facing interface is larger than S, the ITR splits it into two equal fragments and prepends a LISP header to each, so that each encapsulated fragment is S/2 + H octets. The ETR treats the fragments as two separately encapsulated packets, strips the headers and forwards them, and the destination host reassembles them. This behaviour is used only when the source host set the DF field to 0. When the DF field is set to 1, or the packet is IPv6, the ITR drops the packet and returns an ICMPv4 Unreachable / Fragmentation Needed or ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message to the source with a value of S, which is L minus H. When the outer header uses IPv4, an implementation should set the DF bit to 1 so that the ETR does not have to reassemble. It is recommended that L be defined as 1500.

The stateful mechanism keeps track of the effective MTU for each locator in each Map-Cache entry. When an IPv4 encapsulated packet with the DF bit set exceeds what the core network can deliver, an intermediate router sends an ICMPv4 Unreachable / Fragmentation Needed message to the ITR, which works out which locator is affected, records the new effective MTU in the Map-Cache entry, and from then on tells the source the smaller size when a packet exceeds it. The RFC notes that using ICMP for path MTU discovery can behave badly when ICMP packets are lost or spoofed, and points to probe packets and to storing the beginning of large packets as possible mitigations.
sections.plainLanguage: Wrapping a packet makes it bigger, and a bigger packet may not fit on the way. One option is to split the packet in two and let the destination put it back together. The other is to remember the largest packet that fits on each path and to tell the sender when it sends too much.

sections.title: Knowing Whether a Locator Is Up
sections.content:
The RFC lists three data plane ways of learning whether a routing locator can be reached. An ETR may read the Locator-Status-Bits in the header of an encapsulated packet, which tell it the up or down status of the locators at the source site, and use that information when it has traffic to send back. An ETR may also treat the source RLOC in the outer header as likely reachable, although in some scenarios that field can be spoofed. Third, an ITR and ETR pair can use the Echo-Nonce algorithm.

With Echo-Nonce, an ITR that wants to check reachability sets the N-bit and the E-bit and puts a 24-bit nonce in the LISP header of the next encapsulated packet. The ETR forwards the packet as normal, and if it is also acting as an ITR it sends a packet back carrying the nonce with the N-bit set and the E-bit cleared. The ITR sees the echoed nonce and knows the path in both directions is up. If it is receiving packets from the ETR but no nonce comes back while it is in the Echo-Nonce-request state, it concludes the path is down and can switch to another locator. The algorithm is bilateral, so it only works when both devices implement both ITR and ETR functionality, and it does not completely solve the forward path problem because traffic may be one-way.

Locator-Status-Bits work by an ITR telling the ETR which locators in the source site are up. The bits are numbered from 0 to n-1 from the least significant bit of the field, where n is the number of locators in the mapping entry, and the field is 32 bits when the I-bit is zero and 8 bits when it is one. Each ITR at a site can watch the site IGP: under normal circumstances each ITR advertises a default route into it, and if an ITR fails, or its upstream link fails, that default route times out or is withdrawn. An ETR that sees a Locator-Status-Bit change from 1 to 0 refrains from sending to that locator, and resumes when the bit returns to 1.

The Locator-Status-Bits, the Echo-Nonce mechanism and Map-Versioning must not be used over the public Internet, and should only be used in trusted and closed deployments. Locator-Status-Bits should be coupled with Map-Versioning to prevent a race in which the bits are read as referring to different locators than intended.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending to a place, a router may want to know whether that place is working. LISP offers three ways to find out: read a hint that the sending router put in the header, look at who sent the last packet, or send a packet with a random number in it and wait for the number to come back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Gleaning is the optional mechanism that learns a mapping directly from encapsulated packets. Because an off-path attacker can spoof the source EID, traffic destined for the spoofed EID can be diverted, and an attacker who spoofs the source RLOC can mount a denial of service attack by redirecting traffic to it and overloading it.

The reachability mechanisms in the header can also be manipulated. The Locator-Status-Bits, the nonce-present bit and the Echo-Nonce bit can be forged to declare false information about a locator's reachability. One example is an off-path attacker sending data packets to an ITR with a random nonce from a spoofed ETR address, in the hope of convincing the ITR that the ETR's locator is reachable when it is not. The attacker has only a short window in which to guess the nonce the ITR is asking for, and the ITR believes the wrong status until RLOC-Probing detects the correct one, a time frame of the order of tens of seconds. The RFC says this can be mitigated by preventing RLOC spoofing with Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding, and that an ITR which has never asked for a nonce can protect itself by ignoring nonces it did not request. A LISP-specific check is also possible: when decapsulating, an ETR can check that the source EID and RLOC are a valid mapping by consulting the mapping system.

Map-Versioning can be abused too: an attacker can forge the Map-Version field and force an excessive amount of signalling between routers, which may overload them.

The Locator-Status-Bits, the Echo-Nonce mechanism and Map-Versioning must not be used over the public Internet and should only be used in trusted and closed deployments. Deployments that allow fragments of IPv6 encapsulated packets to wait for reassembly at a router should also limit how many fragments are held and how fast they are admitted, so that this does not become a denial of service vector.
sections.plainLanguage: Several of the shortcuts in the data plane can be fooled by someone who is not on the path. A fake source address can send a site's traffic somewhere else, and a fake nonce can make a router believe that a broken path still works. The RFC therefore keeps these mechanisms out of the public internet and recommends checking the source of packets against the mapping system.

items.title: N
items.text: A nonce is present in the first 32-bit field.

items.title: L
items.text: The Locator-Status-Bits in the second field are in use.

items.title: E
items.text: The nonce is to be echoed back.

items.title: V
items.text: A Map-Version is present; the N-bit must then be zero.

items.title: I
items.text: The high-order 24 bits of the second field are an Instance ID.

items.title: R
items.text: Reserved; it must be set to zero on transmit.

items.text: Key identifier used when encapsulated packets are encrypted.
